catalog_quote: The system that exists throughout LC is one of two basic tones, High (H = ') and Low (L = v), which may combine on a given syllable (with restricted and varying distribution) to give Falling (H+L = "), and less frequently, Rising (L+H = ") tones. ... In addition to these two basic tones, there is also a phonologically significant Downstep (Ds = !); i.e., the non-predictable lowering of H following another H ... Lower Cross languages can therefore be characterized as being two-toned, terraced level languages. [p.47] ... Unfortunately, Ward's discussion of stress does not go any deeper than suggesting stress is related to verb stems, and in fact, it is difficult to find any true evidence for stress, at least in the sense proposed by Ward32. [p.55] [fn.32] This is not to assert that there is no stress at all in Efik or the other LC languages. There is likely some sort phrasal stress, and also the juncture between elements of compound words appears to be marked by stress, but these are clearly not what Ward was referring to. Faraclas (1984b) presents an analysis of Obolo incorporating phrasal stress. [p.55] [fn.34] ... as the foot is a notion usually associated with stress phenomena, it is by no means clear how it would apply in a non-stress language. [p.56]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Usaghade, like all Lower Cross languages, is a two-tone (H, L) terraced-level tone language with contrastive downstep; the author finds no evidence for lexical/word-level stress (Ward's 1933 verb-root stress for Efik is rejected) and allows at most phrasal stress and stress at compound junctures; the group is called 'a non-stress language' (fn.34 p.56).
new_statements.exceptions: Possible phrasal stress and stress marking the juncture between elements of compound words (fn.32); Faraclas 1984b posits phrase stress (extra-high tone) for Obolo; Connell 1994 p.12 adds that tone-stress interaction in the group is uninvestigated except for Obolo.
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level statement covering the 19 Lower Cross languages studied (Usakade explicitly among them, p.5; author's own Usakade field recordings), but the stress discussion is framed around Efik (Ward 1933, Cook 1969/1985); no Usaghade-specific stress data. Word vs. phrase: word-level stress denied, phrasal stress allowed.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is Connell's group-level characterization of all Lower Cross languages (19 studied, Usakade = Usaghade [usag1244] explicitly included, p.5, with the author's own Usakade recordings), framed around Efik (Ward 1933); there is no Usaghade-specific stress description anywhere in the accessible literature. Connell's spelling 'Usakade' (1991) = 'Usaghade' (1994, 2001, 2023) = Isangele/Usak Edet; no dialects distinguished.

sources.note: Group-level LC phonology only (Usakade one of 19 languages studied, p.5; own field data). Sec. 2.2.2 p.47: LC languages are 'two-toned, terraced level languages'. Sec. 2.3.3.3 pp.54-55 rejects Ward's (1933) Efik verb-root stress: 'it is difficult to find any true evidence for stress, at least in the sense proposed by Ward'; fn.32 p.55: not asserting no stress at all in Efik or other LC languages, 'likely some sort phrasal stress' and compound-juncture stress; fn.34 p.56 calls LC 'a non-stress language'. No Usakade-specific word-stress statement.

sources.citation: Connell, Bruce. 1994. The Lower Cross languages: a prolegomena to the classification of the Cross River languages. Journal of West African Languages 24(1): 3-46.
sources.note: Sec. 3.3 p.10: all LC languages have two tones H, L plus contrastive downstep; falling tones common in Usaghade among others, from H-spreading. Sec. 5 p.12: 'Tonal systems in the group appear to be further complicated through interaction with phrasal stress, but except for Faraclas (1984b) for Obolo, no investigation in this area has been done.' No word-stress rule for Usaghade.
